articles.title: US Open: Carlos Alcaraz breezes past Tommy Paul in straight sets to advance to quarterfinal
articles.summary: Paul has not been able to snatch a set from Alcaraz since 2024.
articles.body:
Carlos Alcaraz is moving on in the 2026 US Open after a definitive win over Tommy Paul, with the No. 2 ranked player beating the American in straight sets, 6-4, 6-3, 6-4.

In a baffling stat, Sunday's three-set victory marks 14th straight sets that Alcaraz has won against the American. Paul has not taken a set over Alcaraz since Wimbledon in 2024, even though the pair have faced off four times since then.

Though Paul was unable to break through again this time, he did put up a fight in the first set: Alcaraz and Paul traded games until the young Spaniard finally broke the American's serve to eventually win 6-4.

Alcaraz looked like he was on his way to an easy win in the second set, but Paul started to battle back, fighting off multiple break points before Alcaraz was able to hold him off.

Paul fought another break from Alcaraz in the the third game of the set, scoring three unanswered points to claw back from a near-scoreless game. But Alcaraz recovered well to snatch the break point and send him on the path to victory.

With Alcaraz one game from a win — and Paul failing to pick up a single break in the third — Paul was able to sweep through his final service game without letting Alcaraz snatch a point back. However, the American couldn't hold off Alcaraz as the Spaniard used his power to deftly finish Paul off.

Alcaraz has barely missed a step since returning from a wrist injury that sidelined him for 4 ½ months. The Spaniard kicked things off with a strong showing , beating Roman Safiullin in straight sets ; though he dropped the first set to Jaime Faria in the second round, he pulled back for another win , and then beat Wu Yibing in straight sets as well.

Initially, Alcaraz's return, paired with World No. 1 Jannik Sinner pulling out of the tournament with a knee injury, left the impression of a wide-open bracket in men's singles . But even after a long layoff, Alcaraz is continuing his dominance: He is now 63-0 in major tournaments after winning the first two sets.

Alcaraz will now continue his journey toward trying to defend his 2025 US Open title in the quarterfinal, facing the winner of Sunday night's match between No. 8 Ben Shelton and Stefanos Tsitsipas.

Paul, meanwhile, will fall out of a Grand Slam before the quarterfinal for the sixth consecutive tournament, with his last quarterfinal appearance coming at Roland-Garros in 2025.

articles.title: Alcaraz delivers statement win to reach last eight
articles.summary: Carlos Alcaraz continues his return from long-term injury with a hugely impressive fourth-round win against Tommy Paul at the US Open.
articles.body:
Carlos Alcaraz continued his return from long-term injury with a hugely impressive fourth-round win against Tommy Paul at the US Open.

Playing just his fourth competitive singles match after an absence of more than four months, the 23-year-old Spaniard produced a masterful performance to beat American 20th seed Paul 6-4 6-3 6-4.

He has dropped only one set on his way to the last eight in New York and his quarter-final opponent will be either American eighth seed Ben Shelton or Greece's Stefanos Tsitsipas.

A wrist injury caused Alcaraz to miss both the French Open and Wimbledon earlier this summer.

He had won the previous two Grand Slams - last year's US Open and this year's Australian Open - meaning the straight-set victory over Paul extended his run of match wins at the majors to 18.

Asked on court if he is back to "full power", Alcaraz smiled as he replied: "I think so. Except for one year since [his US Open debut in] 2021, I've made the quarter-finals here. That shows how special this place is to me and shows how well I'm playing every time I come here.

"I just try to enjoy my time on the court and it doesn't matter that I was out for four and a half months - every time I come here, I play my best."

Shelton and Tsitsipas meet in Sunday's night session and seven-time major champion Alcaraz has never previously lost to either player at Tour level, beating Shelton three times and Tsitsipas on six occasions.

"If Shelton were to come through, he is the kind of player that can knock the racquet out of your hand," said American former player Jeff Tarango on BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra.

"It's going to be a real test to see how Alcaraz's wrist is with a 149mph serve coming to that forehand, but Alcaraz should get through Shelton if his wrist is fine."

Alcaraz said after his third-round win that he was happy with the level of fitness he had shown in the early rounds following his lengthy absence, while he demonstrated against Paul that the quality of his shot-making is as good as ever.

One sensational cross-court forehand winner early in the second set, which landed in from an almost impossible angle, was measured at 103mph.

That came shortly after Alcaraz had broken Paul's serve in the 10th game of a tight, high-quality opening set to take it 6-4.

Paul, who was attempting to reach the quarter-finals of his home Grand Slam for the first time, battled hard throughout but Alcaraz proved to be too strong.

Paul had two break points when Alcaraz served for the match at 5-4 in the third set, but the two-time US Open champion put together a run of four straight points to seal victory.

Former British number one Tim Henman told Sky Sports: "When you haven't played tennis for four weeks, it seems a lot and you can be a bit rusty. This is four and a half months.

"If you would have given Alcaraz a blank piece of paper at the beginning of the tournament and asked how he'd want the first four matches to go, he would have scripted it exactly like that.

"He's had a few slightly challenging moments but, in the important moments, he's just come up with incredible tennis. That's got to give him so much confidence moving forward."

articles.title: Wimbledon won't credential influencers, already taking precautions after US Open issues
articles.summary: Influencers and content creators have been all over the US Open this fall, and it's caused some disruptions to the Grand Slam.
articles.body:
There won't be a swarm of influencers at Wimbledon next summer after how things have gone so far at the US Open.

Wimbledon does not plan to allow an influx of influencers at the Grand Slam next summer, according to The Press Association . Security will confiscate items, like ring lights, that could be used to disrupt matches, and Wimbledon will not have any accreditation category for influencers or content creators.

That is in stark contrast to the US Open this fall, which has seen plenty of influencers and other content creators throughout the tournament. That's caused multiple issues already.

While the US Open has traditionally had the rowdiest crowd among the four Grand Slams, the influencer debate has taken off throughout the tournament. Roughly 100 influencers and content creators were credentialed as media this year, nearly twice as many from 2025. A pair of influencers had their credentials revoked , too.

People have been creating content at the tournament during matches, including staging photoshoots and bringing in lighting. Naomi Osaka's first-round match even had to be paused.

While that has brought a lot of added attention to both the tournament and the sport in general, many players have spoken out about the disruptions.

"I feel like it's common courtesy to read up on the sport, especially the etiquette. I feel like it could be a good thing for people to make the sport of tennis popular to their specific audience, but I think it has to be managed a lot better, especially in the situation like in my first-round match," Osaka said after that incident. "Overall, I think there's huge positives. … You want people to continue to grow the sport. I just think it has to be in a way that everyone knows the rules and the etiquette."

There has also been the odor of marijuana, which is legal recreationally in New York, occasionally during the tournament.

"People are allowed to move around in the crowd during points," France's Adrian Mannarino said, via The Press Association. "The tournament puts up with it, and I don't know if it's the best thing for tennis in general.

"There's a smell of marijuana on the court, noise everywhere. The truth is, it's turning into a bit of a zoo."

While Wimbledon is still about 10 months away, the tournament is apparently already preparing to keep things calm in London next summer.

articles.title: Watch Carlos Alcaraz Not Know Next Opponent in US Open Bracket During Funny Video
articles.summary: Carlos Alcaraz was surprised to find out who he would be playing in the quarterfinal of the US Open.
articles.body:
Carlos Alcaraz was surprised to find out who he would be playing in the quarterfinal of the US Open.

The star tennis player was shocked when told he'd be facing either Ben Shelton or Stefanos Tsitsipas during a live interview on ESPN, as he thought he was going up against Frances Tiafoe.

Tiafoe will instead go up against Alex Michelsen, while Alcaraz will have to wait until later on Sunday for his opponent to be decided.

No matter who he faces, Alcaraz will be the presumed favorite. The defending US Open champion has thrived in his return to tennis after several months off, losing just one set in his first four matches in New York.

He beat Tommy Paul 6-4, 6-3, 6-4 on Sunday to advance to the quarterfinal, and he'll look to carry his momentum into his next match, which will be on Tuesday.

Luckily for Alcaraz, he was informed of his potential opponent before Sunday's match between Shelton and Tsitsipas, so he'll have the chance to watch and prepare for his next match.

articles.title: Who are Iga Swiatek’s parents? Meet Tomasz Swiatek, Olympic rower dad, and orthodontist mom Dorota
articles.summary: International Sports News: Iga Swiatek’s rise to the top of women’s tennis has been shaped by a family with sporting and professional roots. Her father, Tomasz Swiatek, represen.
articles.body: Iga Swiatek’s rise to the top of women’s tennis has been shaped by a family with sporting and professional roots. Her father, Tomasz Swiatek, represented Poland in rowing at the 1988 Seoul Olympics, while her mother, Dorota Swiatek, built a career as an orthodontist. Iga has also credited her older sister, Agata Swiatek, with inspiring her to pick up tennis. From sibling rivalry to years of coaching from her father, the family played a role in her development. Here’s a closer look at Iga Swiatek’s parents, sister and the influence they had on her career.Tomasz Swiatek shaped Iga’s sporting pathTomasz Swiatek was an accomplished athlete before his daughter became one of tennis’s biggest names. He competed for Poland in the men’s quadruple sculls at the 1988 Summer Olympics in Seoul. His experience in elite sport gave him an understanding of training, discipline and competition, which later became useful as Iga developed her own career.Tomasz encouraged both of his daughters, Agata and Iga, to become involved in sport. However, he wanted them to choose an individual discipline rather than a team sport. Iga initially tried swimming but did not enjoy it because she was afraid of the water. Tennis soon became the better fit.In interviews, Iga has explained that her older sister played a key role in that decision. Agata, who is three years older, was already playing tennis, and Iga wanted to follow her example. Their competitive relationship also pushed Iga forward. She recalled that she often competed with Agata when they were younger and usually lost, which gave her extra motivation to improve.Iga eventually turned that early rivalry into a professional career. She started playing tennis at around six or seven and quickly showed the ability to compete at a high level. In 2020, she made history by becoming the first Polish player to win a Grand Slam singles title when she captured the French Open.Tomasz remained closely involved throughout much of that journey. He served as the head of Iga’s coaching team until 2024, before stepping back to give his daughter greater independence. Even after leaving that formal role, he has continued to support her at tournaments and speak publicly about her career.Dorota and Agata built careers away from tennisWhile Tomasz and Iga became closely associated with competitive sport, Dorota Swiatek followed a different professional path. She is an orthodontist and has worked in the field since 1991. Her professional work focuses on orthodontic treatment, including dental alignment problems and other defects.Dorota has also emphasized that her daughter’s happiness matters more to her than trophies. In a 2020 interview with Polish outlet Super Express, she said she was proud of Iga’s achievements but cared most about seeing her do something she genuinely loved. She was also not shocked by Iga’s breakthrough at the 2020 French Open, having watched her development for many years.Agata followed their mother into the medical profession. After playing junior tennis, she stopped competing around 2015-2016 after an injury. She later graduated from the Medical University of Lublin in 2022 and began working as a dentist, with an interest in periodontology.Despite taking different professional paths, the Swiatek family has remained closely connected. Iga’s story shows how her parents provided support in different ways, while her sister’s example helped spark the competitive drive that eventually took her to the biggest stages in tennis.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Who are Jessica Pegula’s parents? Meet billionaire dad Terry and Kim Pegula, the family behind her tennis career
articles.summary: International Sports News: Jessica Pegula’s tennis career has been backed by two parents who built very different lives before becoming known around the sports world. Her father.
articles.body: Jessica Pegula’s tennis career has been backed by two parents who built very different lives before becoming known around the sports world. Her father, Terry Pegula, made his fortune in oil and gas before becoming the owner of the Buffalo Bills and Buffalo Sabres. Her mother, Kim Pegula, was born in South Korea and adopted by a New York family as a child before building a career in sports. The couple encouraged Jessica to play tennis from age seven and moved their family to support her training. Their support has remained important throughout her career.Terry and Kim Pegula supported Jessica Pegula’s tennis from an early ageTerry and Kim began encouraging Jessica to play tennis when she was 7. She was born in Buffalo, N.Y., and the family later moved to Wexford, Pa., South Carolina and Florida as Jessica focused more seriously on the sport.Jessica has said her parents put her tennis ahead of their connection to professional sports. Kim summed up that attitude in a 2019 interview with WKBW-TV after Jessica won the Citi Open.“We always say she’s our first sports team and our favorite,” Kim said.Terry studied petroleum and natural gas engineering at Penn State before working in the oil industry. In 1983, he started East Resources after borrowing $7,500 from family and friends. He later sold most of the company’s assets to Royal Dutch Shell for $4.7 billion in 2010, according to Forbes.The Pegulas then moved into professional sports. They bought the Buffalo Sabres in 2011 and became owners of the Buffalo Bills in 2014.Kim’s story is very different. She was born in Seoul and was adopted by Ralph and Marilyn Kerr when she was 5. She grew up in Fairport, N.Y., and graduated from Houghton College in 1991 with a communications degree.Jessica has also spoken about how her parents handled her tennis career. In a 2021 Bills Pod Squad interview, she described Terry as “old school” and said he always pushed her to work harder. She described Kim as more focused on life away from the court, including diet, recovery and training.Kim Pegula’s journey and her family’s support for JessicaKim’s background has also shaped Jessica’s connection to her heritage. After winning the 2023 Korea Open in Seoul, Jessica wrote on X that the victory was “extra special” because she is half Korean. She said she was still learning about her culture and was moved by the support from Korean fans.The family went through a difficult period in 2022 when Kim suffered cardiac arrest. Jessica later wrote in The Players’ Tribune that her family spent about two weeks at the hospital and that Terry stayed close to Kim during her recovery. NHL.com also reported on Jessica’s 2023 update about her mother’s recovery.Jessica has been clear that her parents’ influence was not simply about money or access to sports. “My parents have helped me achieve this dream I am living,” she wrote. “Even though we didn’t always agree, they pushed me, and I pushed back, and it got me to where I am today.”They gave Jessica the chance to pursue tennis, pushed her when needed and supported her away from the court. Jessica went on to become one of the leading American players of her generation, while her parents remained closely connected to her journey.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Newspaper headlines: 'Losing battle to halt Russia's 'hybrid' war' and 'Oh chute!'
articles.summary: A warning from defence officials and a skydiving miracle lead Monday's front pages.
articles.body:
The Daily Telegraph reports that the British Chambers of Commerce has called for the pension triple lock to be scrapped in a bid to help, what the paper refers to as, Britain's "ailing economy". The business group, which represents more than 65,000 firms, suggests the savings should be used to tackle youth unemployment.

The Financial Times carries a warning from intelligence officials that Europe is "losing the battle" to stop Russia's "hybrid" war against the continent. Experts say last month's failed drone attack on Leipzig airport should serve as a "wake up call". Moscow has denied any involvement.

"Just 1% of asylum pleas are genuine", is the headline on the front page of the Times. An anonymous whistleblower, described as a Home Office official, has told the paper that asylum seekers from certain countries are using the "same script". The Home Office says asylum claims are considered on an individual basis, and processes are in place to assess their credibility.

The i Paper leads on the former Labour cabinet minister Lord Blunkett, who's urging Andy Burnham to "find the money to fund end-of-life care ". He's joined a call, backed by almost 300 MPs and peers, to boost funding for hospices, which are facing a £745m gap. The Department of Health has previously said it will continue to support hospices.

According to the Daily Telegraph the " scourge of the tennis influencer " will not be coming to Wimbledon. The All England Club is set to take a stand, after various distractions at the US Open. These have included people taking photographs using bright lighting, and too much noise during points, much to the annoyance of players.

And a couple of the papers report on a museum in the United States revealing its latest acquisition, red leather sofas once used by visitors to the National Gallery in London. The Daily Telegraph and the Times both say the pieces were sold after being deemed a fire risk, and difficult to clean. But it hasn't stopped the Wadsworth Atheneum in Connecticut proudly posting a photograph of its new furnishings, with the caption "your seat awaits".

Also on the paper's front page, it reports that the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party is on course to win a regional election. It says the right-wing AfD is projected to become the largest party in Saxony-Anhalt but is expected to fall short of a parliamentary majority.

articles.title: Inspiring story of the day: “My grandfather always told me to focus on the Three Cs: Cabeza, Corazón y Cojones” - How Carlos Alcaraz turned three generations of family love into tennis immortality
articles.summary: International Sports News: Carlos Alcaraz’s rise to seven Grand Slam titles has been shaped by more than his talent on the tennis court. A lesson from his grandfather, Carlos Al.
articles.body: Carlos Alcaraz’s rise to seven Grand Slam titles has been shaped by more than his talent on the tennis court. A lesson from his grandfather, Carlos Alcaraz Lerma, became one of the most personal parts of his career: “Cabeza, corazón y cojones” - head, heart and courage. Alcaraz later had the three Cs tattooed on his wrist as a reminder of that message. His close relationship with former world No. 1 Juan Carlos Ferrero also played a major role in his development. Together, those family and coaching ties helped shape the player who became the youngest man to complete the Career Grand Slam in 2026.What did Carlos Alcaraz’s grandfather teach him about the Three CsThe phrase came from Alcaraz’s grandfather and stayed with him as he grew up in El Palmar, Murcia. The three words are “Cabeza, corazón y cojones”, which mean head, heart and courage, with the final Spanish word being a much stronger and more informal expression.For Alcaraz, the idea was simple. He needed his head to make the right decisions, his heart to play with passion and courage to take risks when the pressure was highest.Alcaraz has spoken about the message before, saying:“My grandfather always told me to focus on the Three Cs: head, heart, and balls.”The words became closely linked with his identity as a player. His tennis is built around attacking shots, quick movement and a willingness to try difficult plays even when a match is going against him.The story also has a strong family connection. Alcaraz’s grandfather was involved with tennis in El Palmar, where the young player spent part of his early years around the sport.That makes the “Three Cs” more than a slogan. It is a piece of advice that Alcaraz has carried from his childhood into the biggest matches of his career.Why did Carlos Alcaraz get the Three Cs tattooAfter breaking through at the highest level, Alcaraz chose to keep his grandfather’s message with him permanently. In 2022, he got a CCC tattoo, representing “Cabeza, Corazón y Cojones.”The tattoo became a visible reminder of the words that had followed him through his early tennis career. Reports at the time said the tattoo was placed on his wrist and was connected directly to his grandfather’s motto.The timing was also significant. Alcaraz had just enjoyed the breakthrough season that changed his career. He won his first Masters 1000 title in Miami in April 2022 and then won his first Grand Slam at the US Open later that year.By September 2022, he had also become the youngest player to reach No. 1 in the ATP rankings at 19 years and four months. He finished that season as the youngest year-end No. 1 in ATP history.The tattoo therefore came during the period when Alcaraz was moving from a highly rated teenager to one of the biggest names in tennis.Rather than choosing a trophy or a tournament date, he picked something tied to his family.How did Juan Carlos Ferrero become like a second father to Carlos AlcarazAlcaraz’s grandfather gave him the message, but Juan Carlos Ferrero became one of the most important people in turning that young talent into a top-level player.Ferrero, a former world No. 1 and 2003 French Open champion, began working with Alcaraz when the Spaniard was a teenager. Alcaraz trained at Ferrero’s academy in Villena, Spain, and their relationship grew far beyond normal coach-player duties.Alcaraz has openly described Ferrero as his mentor and second father.“He was my mentor. Everything that I’ve done is thanks to him. I learned a lot, not only professionally, but the personal part as well. He’s my second father… I am the person and the player I am today thanks to him.”Those comments came after years of working together. Ferrero also described Alcaraz as being like a fourth child to him, showing how close the relationship had become.One of the most emotional moments in their relationship came in 2022. Ferrero’s father, Eduardo Ferrero, died suddenly in March while Juan Carlos was in the United States with Alcaraz. Ferrero returned to Spain for the funeral before coming back to Miami, where Alcaraz was preparing for the tournament final.Alcaraz went on to beat Casper Ruud 7-5, 6-4 in the Miami final to win his first Masters 1000 title. Afterward, the two shared an emotional moment.Their professional partnership eventually ended in December 2025 after about seven years. Even then, Alcaraz made clear how much Ferrero had meant to his career, calling their time together an important chapter of his life.How have Carlos Alcaraz’s family lessons followed him into tennis historyThe clearest proof of Alcaraz’s growth came in 2026.He entered the Australian Open without a title at Melbourne Park, but defeated Novak Djokovic in the final to win his seventh Grand Slam. That victory completed all four major titles for Alcaraz: the US Open, Wimbledon, Roland Garros and Australian Open.At 22 years and 272 days, he became the youngest man to complete the Career Grand Slam in the Open Era.His Grand Slam record now includes two US Open titles, two Wimbledon titles, two French Open titles and one Australian Open title.Even with those achievements, the idea behind the Three Cs remains easy to understand. Head is about making good decisions. Heart is about loving the game. Courage is about taking the shot when the moment demands it.That message began with his grandfather and became part of Alcaraz’s identity long before he was winning major trophies. His tattoo keeps those words close, while the years with Ferrero helped him learn how to handle the pressure that comes with becoming a champion.And now, at 23, Alcaraz is already a seven-time major winner and a Career Grand Slam champion. His records have grown, but the family lesson behind the three letters has stayed remarkably simple.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: El arte en peligro de extinción en el tenis: el revés a una mano desaparece 150 años después
articles.standfirst: Por primera vez en 150 años ningún jugador con revés a una mano alcanzará las semifinales de un Grand Slam
articles.summary: Por primera vez en 150 años ningún jugador con revés a una mano alcanzará las semifinales de un Grand Slam
articles.body: Con la eliminación del griego Stefanos Tsitsipas en los octavos de final del Abierto de Estados Unidos ante Ben Shelton, ya es seguro que, por primera vez en 150 años, ningún jugador con revés a una mano alcanzará las semifinales de un Grand Slam. "Tengo una racha de 150 años que salvar", escribió recientemente Tsitsipas en sus redes sociales, al referirse a este dato y al 'peligro de extinción' del revés a una mano. No pudo hacerlo. Se rindió por 6-2, 6-3 y 6-4 ante Ben Shelton, que será el próximo rival del español Carlos Alcaraz en los cuartos de final. Tsitsipas es uno de los cada vez menos jugadores del circuito ATP que utilizan el revés a una mano. Se une al italiano Lorenzo Musetti, el canadiense Denis Shapovalov y el búlgaro Grigor Dimitrov, todos ya eliminados en Nueva York. Hasta el legendario Roger Federer, que hizo maravillas con su icónico revés a una mano, analizó la crisis de este golpe. "Me encanta ver cuando a los jugadores de revés a una mano les va bien. Cuando crecía, diría que el 90% de mis entrenadores tenían revés a una mano. Creo que, cuando tu entrenador juega el revés a una mano, es muy probable que tú también acabes jugándolo así. Hoy en día, probablemente la mayoría de los entrenadores juegan el revés a dos manos, y es más fácil enseñarle a un niño a golpear el revés con dos manos", reflexionó. articles.title: Sabalenka overcomes tricky Townsend test at US Open
articles.summary: Two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka emulates Serena Williams by overcoming Taylor Townsend to reach a sixth straight US Open quarter-final.
articles.body:
Two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka emulated Serena Williams as she eventually overpowered American Taylor Townsend to reach a sixth straight US Open quarter-final.

A topsy-turvy contest featured 10 breaks of serve, but Sabalenka recovered from 3-1 down in the second set to seal a 6-4 6-3 victory with a fifth consecutive game.

It was the Belarusian's 18th consecutive win at the tournament, extending her three-year unbeaten streak following back-to-back triumphs in 2024 and 2025.

Sabalenka, 28, is the first woman to reach six consecutive singles quarter-finals at Flushing Meadows since American great Williams in 2016.

Six-time champion Williams was also the last player to win three US Open titles in a row, and Sabalenka is now three wins from matching that feat.

She will face Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova for a semi-final place, after the Czech sixth seed required six match points to overcome Ukraine's Marta Kostyuk in a rollercoaster 7-5 5-7 6-4 win.

Despite the straightforward scoreline this was a tricky match which required a resilient display from Sabalenka, who also had the vast majority of the crowd against her.

In that context this was an impressive victory for the four-time major winner, who has not always managed to maintain her composure in similarly testing scenarios.

"I was just trying to stay focused on myself, not only point by point but ball by ball," Sabalenka said.

"I'm happy I was able to turn around the second set, I think it was a key moment."

The match began with five successive breaks of serve - mostly due to excellent returning by both players - but it was Sabalenka who finally took charge.

Doubles specialist Townsend, who walked out wearing a long, black-feathered outfit, continued to frustrate Sabalenka and forced her to serve out the set at the second opportunity, before making the breakthrough in the second set.

But Sabalenka, aware she must lift the trophy to have a chance of retaining her number one ranking, produced an immediate reply as she broke back to love and dashed to the finish line, wrapping up the victory in 75 minutes.

Pegula wins to bring curtain down on Cirstea's Grand Slam career

American third seed Jessica Pegula brought the curtain down on Sorana Cirstea's Grand Slam career with a 6-3 6-4 win over the Romanian.

Cirstea is set to retire at the end of 2026, despite it being one of the best seasons of her 20-year career.

In May, the 36-year-old became the oldest player in rankings history to make her top 20 debut and she is currently ranked at a career-high 17th following a run to the quarter-finals at the French Open.

She also reached the third round at the Australian Open and Wimbledon, while she lifted the fourth WTA title of her career at her home tournament in Cluj-Napoca.

But Cirstea missed out on a third major quarter-final as Pegula came through a tricky test that saw 11 breaks of serve, securing victory on her third match point.

"I just told her I don't know if you're still going to play next year, but you are playing great and I said I have a lot of respect for you," Pegula said when asked what she told Cirstea when they shared an embrace at the net.

Pegula, the 2024 runner-up to Sabalenka, will continue her chase for a third straight US Open semi-final when she faces fellow American Emma Navarro, who defeated Russian Anna Kalinskaya 6-4 6-2.

Earlier on Sunday, Noskova's sense of relief was cleared as she crouched to the ground after taking her sixth match point about an hour after earning her first.

The 21-year-old served for the match in the second set, but missed her first two match points as Kostyuk battled back from 5-3 down to force a decider.

Noskova failed to take her next two match points in the decider, while she missed her fifth match point after saving a break point, before finally getting over the line after an emotionally draining two and a half hours on court.

"I am more than relieved, this match was so tough, emotionally a bit more than physically," said Noskova, who missed five championship points before lifting the Wimbledon title this summer.

"Today was very close, it could have ended both ways. With all the chances I had in the second set, it was tough to still kind of restart."

In the women's doubles, British pair Harriet Dart and Maia Lumsden lost 6-2 6-2 to Spain's Cristina Bucsa and American Nicole Melichar-Martinez, the sixth seeds.

articles.title: ‘This is not sustainable’: US Open’s post-2 am finishes spark player backlash as Navratilova, Becker question late-night scheduling
articles.summary: Tennis News: The US Open’s famous late-night energy is once again coming under scrutiny, but this time the concern is not about whether New York can keep the party.
articles.body: The US Open’s famous late-night energy is once again coming under scrutiny, but this time the concern is not about whether New York can keep the party going. It is about whether the players can.As the first week of the Grand Slam winds down, a growing number of matches have stretched well past midnight, with three of the first six night sessions finishing after 2 am (local time) and two others extending beyond 1 am. The unusually late endings have prompted four-time US Open singles champion Martina Navratilova, six-time Grand Slam winner Boris Becker and several players to question whether the scheduling has gone too far.Navratilova was among the most direct in her criticism, posting on X after the tournament recorded three post-2 am finishes in its opening six days."This is not sustainable…": Navratilova wrote while sharing statistics highlighting the late finishes.Becker, the 1989 US Open champion, also weighed in after Navratilova's post, questioning why tennis players are being asked to compete at such hours."That’s simple to late to play tennis ?? anymore….tell me another sport like that ?!?," Becker posted.The issue has become particularly noticeable in a tournament where night tennis has long been part of its identity. Arthur Ashe Stadium under the lights, packed stands and an electric New York crowd are among the defining images of the US Open. But as matches increasingly spill into the early hours, players and former champions are beginning to question where the line should be drawn.‘Everybody wants to go to sleep’Alexander Zverev had little appetite for an extended discussion after his first-round match ended in the early hours. With empty seats visible around the court, the German top seed took just two questions from reporters before making his feelings clear."I think everybody's tired," he said. "Everybody wants to go to sleep."The problem became even more pronounced for Zverev as the tournament progressed. His first two matches finished at 1:55 am and 2:15 am, respectively, making him the first top-seeded man to play back-to-back five-set matches to begin a major in the Open era, which dates back to 1968.His experience has underlined the physical cost of the scheduling, particularly when players have to recover from long matches and then prepare for the next round within a limited window.Pegula questions whether it is ‘the right thing’Third-ranked women's player Jessica Pegula acknowledged that tournament organisers have to balance several competing demands, including television schedules and match timings. But she questioned whether those considerations should come at the expense of players having to compete deep into the night."I know they're dealing with a lot of different aspects as far as broadcast and TV and making sure certain matches get done and are starting at a certain time for those reasons," Pegula said."But you have to wonder if it's really the right thing for players to be finishing at 2 am, especially when it’s not — like, I'm not watching on TV. I'm sleeping. Some people stay, but there is a lot of people that need to go home."Her comments reflect a broader concern around the sustainability of the current schedule. A late finish does not simply mean a player leaves the court later. It can affect meals, recovery, sleep and preparation for the following day.Other Grand Slam tournaments have taken different approaches. Wimbledon has instituted an 11 pm curfew, while the French Open schedules only one match during its night session.The US Open, meanwhile, has traditionally embraced the possibility of matches running deep into the night. This year's schedule, however, has pushed that tradition to an extreme.Venus Williams caught in historic late startThe issue was apparent from the opening night itself.Novak Djokovic's first-round match lasted four hours and 36 minutes on August 30. The length of that contest pushed Venus Williams and Sofia Kenin onto court at 12:13 am, the latest match start in US Open history.Much of the crowd stayed to watch what could have been the 46-year-old Williams' final Grand Slam singles match. But the timing made the occasion more difficult for both players."It's not ideal," Williams said. "I would have preferred something else, definitely. It wasn't great for either of us, so I think we both tried our best. I just don't know any other sport where you have to start that late. I definitely think there's room for improvement there."The match eventually concluded at 2:01 am, adding another chapter to a tournament already seeing an unusual number of after-midnight finishes.Shelton experiences his first 2 am finishBen Shelton also found himself dealing with the consequences of the scheduling when his second-round match against Denis Shapovalov, which began on Friday night, finished at 2:07 am Saturday.The delay was partly caused by the Williams sisters' doubles match, which lasted more than three hours."Not easy," Shelton said after defeating Shapovalov in 3 hours, 22 minutes. "My first time experiencing playing this late."Shelton estimated that he would not get to sleep until around 5 am, highlighting how a match that ends after 2 am can effectively consume much of the following morning as well.Four of the 17 latest finishes in US Open history have now occurred this year. The tournament record remains 2:50 am, set in 2022 when Carlos Alcaraz defeated Jannik Sinner in the quarterfinals on his way to his first US Open title.Sabalenka warns of disrupted schedulesTop-ranked Aryna Sabalenka, who two years ago played what was then the fourth-latest women's match in tournament history, has also experienced the knock-on effects of finishing after midnight.She is not a fan of such late starts and the disruption they can cause to an athlete's routine."When you finish late, the next day shifts a lot," Sabalenka said. "Like, you still need to get your hours of sleep, so you start later. You just can really mess up your schedule."That is at the heart of the debate surrounding the US Open's night sessions. The spectacle of late-night tennis can be a major attraction for fans, broadcasters and the tournament itself. But for the athletes, a match finishing at 2 am can have consequences that extend well beyond the final point.With four of the latest 17 finishes in tournament history already coming this year, the question is no longer simply whether New York's tennis nights can continue deep into the morning.It is whether they should.For Navratilova, the answer appears increasingly clear: "This is not sustainable…".Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Alexandra Eala: Coco Gauff struggles to relate to pressure on rising Filipino star
articles.summary: World number four Coco Gauff says she "can't really empathise" with rising Filipino star Alexandra Eala because "she has more pressure than I do".
articles.body:
World number four Coco Gauff says she "can't really empathise" with rising Filipino star Alexandra Eala because "she has more pressure than I do".

Eala became the first Filipino to win a WTA singles title last month and has risen to 18th in the world rankings.

After losing to Iva Jovic in the third round of the US Open, the 21-year-old got emotional when talking about the huge support she gets from the Philippines.

Gauff will now meet Jovic in the fourth round and the 22-year-old American was asked if she can relate to what Eala, with whom she has played doubles, has to cope with.

"No, I can't at all, because she's the first Filipino player to break a lot of the barriers that she's done, especially on the female side," said Gauff, a two-time Grand Slam winner.

"When you speak of athletes from the Philippines, she's doing similar things to what Manny Pacquiao is doing for her country.

"I'm lucky to be from the US, where we had a lot of icons to look up to, people who have already broken down doors for me to be here where I am.

"I can't really empathise in that aspect. The only way I can is maybe just the hype of everyone expecting you to win every single match."

On her US Open debut last year, Eala became the first Filipino player to win a match during the Open era, and has this year reached the fourth round at Wimbledon as well as the third round at Flushing Meadows.

After Wimbledon, she returned home to a reception held by Filipino president Ferdinand Marcos in her honour at Malacanang Palace in Manila.

Eala won her second WTA 125 singles title at Birmingham in June before claiming her maiden WTA 500 title at the Washington Open, with Filipino fans and flags becoming more prominent at her matches.

"From the outside looking in, she has more pressure," Gauff added.

"I have a lot of respect for her and what she's doing, but I can't really empathise. I feel like she has more pressure than I do."

articles.title: Federer, Sampras, Kuerten... no one: After 149 years, end of an era in tennis
articles.summary: Tennis News: NEW DELHI: \"I've got a 150-year streak to save,\" Stefanos Tsitsipas wrote in an X post on Saturday. The Greek tennis player tends to post hyperbole, v.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: "I've got a 150-year streak to save," Stefanos Tsitsipas wrote in an X post on Saturday. The Greek tennis player tends to post hyperbole, veering from the philosophical to the absurd. But here, for a change, he was spot on. As he faced Ben Shelton in the fourth round of the US Open, he was indeed playing to keep one of tennis' biggest traditions alive. A tradition that started in 1877 at the All England Lawn Tennis & Croquet Club culminated in a New York evening at Arthur Ashe Stadium in 2026.For the first time since Grand Slam tennis began in 1877 at Wimbledon, no man with a one-handed backhand will reach a major semi-final in a season.At first, the one-handed backhand was the default choice. With wooden rackets, amateurs and professionals alike would employ a single-handed backhand to outfox their opponents.When the game evolved, two-handed backhands found their groove. The number of one-handed backhand players reduced, but the stroke still maintained its presence. John McEnroe, Ivan Lendl, Stefan Edberg, Pete Sampras, Gustavo Kuerten, Richard Gasquet, Roger Federer, Stan Wawrinka and Dominic Thiem are some of the names that have embraced the stroke over the last four decades or more.In 1905, when all four Slams were played, there were 16 one-handed backhanders in Grand Slam semifinals. Jump a grand hundred years to 2005, and that number had reduced to five. Federer, four times, and Mariano Puerta made up that list. Last year, that number dwindled to just one, with Lorenzo Musetti reaching the last four of the French Open.The 24-year-old Italian is the highest-ranked single-handed backhand men's player in the ATP standings. But he couldn't carry this 149-year-old legacy forward, going out in the second round of the US Open. Neither could Canada's Denis Shapovalov, World No. 48, who bowed out to Ben Shelton in the third round. Nor could 2016 US Open champion Stan Wawrinka, who was handed a late wildcard, exiting and retiring after a first-round loss.Earlier this year, Musetti could have kept that streak going in Melbourne. He was up by two sets in the quarter-final against Novak Djokovic at the Australian Open. Leading 6-4, 6-3, he injured his upper right leg and was unable to continue despite a visit from the physio.'Like dinosaurs going extinct'There are 19 one-handed backhanders in the ATP top-300 rankings. In 2013, that number stood at 62 across the ATP and Challenger levels.“Every single decade, we’re decreasing. We’re like dinosaurs going extinct,” said Tsitsipas, a two-time major finalist, after his second-round win over Lloyd Harris.Musetti acknowledges that the changing shape of the sport has been a key reason. “I think it is partly a consequence of the fact that, realistically, the two-handed backhand offers an advantage in modern tennis,” said Musetti, who reached major semifinals in 2024 and 2025.I think when your coach is a one-handed tennis player, you will most likely be a one-handed tennis player tooFederer, who won 20 major titles in his trophy-laden career, says the early days of a tennis player make a difference.“I think when your coach is a one-handed tennis player, you will most likely be a one-handed tennis player too,” the Swiss said before the US Open. “Nowadays, probably the coaches are mostly double-handed players, and it's just easier to teach a kid to have two hands on the backhand side. One of my kids is switching from a double-hander to a one-hander, and I just see how hard it is for him to hit it and control it.”Then there is Diane Parry. The Frenchwoman uses a two-handed backhand when returning serve before reverting to a one-hander, something that 'suits her soul'.“I thought that it might perhaps help me, because, when you think about it, it is still easier to return a fast serve with two hands,” she said during the US Open. “It does not come naturally to me, though, so it requires work, and it takes time before everything falls properly into place. But it remains an option in my game.”Denis Shapovalov advocates for the one-hander, given the opportunity to create better angles compared with the two-handed backhand. Musetti, meanwhile, acknowledges that the two-handed backhand is "more advantageous today", even though he intends to teach it as a father or coach.“Aesthetically, yes, I would teach it. I would love for my son, or perhaps a player I coach in the future, to have a one-handed backhand. I would love to see that.“But in terms of efficiency, I think the two-handed backhand is more advantageous, especially in the modern game, with the speed at which tennis is played today,” stated the 24-year-old Italian.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.body: Carlos Alcaraz se fijaba en Roger Federer y Rafael Nadal en el momento de afrontar el Abierto de los Estados Unidos después de una ausencia de 139 días provocado por una lesión en la muñeca derecha. "Federer y Nadal demostraron que es posible ganar un Grand Slam después de estar mucho tiempo parados", recordaba. Alcaraz, flamante cuartofinalista del torneo neoyorquino tras derrotar al local Tommy Paul, ya firma el mejor regreso en el circuito desde que Nadal se coronó por partido doble en Melbourne en enero de 2022. El balear se anotó primer el Open 250 preparatorio, también celebrado en las pistas de Flinders Park, y, posteriormente, levantó el trofeo Norman Brookes del primer grande del calendario al remontar dos sets a Daniil Medvedev. La remontada de Rafa desafió a toda lógica ya que la probabilidad de victoria del español era de tan sólo el 4 por ciento después de ceder las dos primeras mangas. A esa cifra se agarró para sumar el vigésimo primer 'major' de su carrera. Carlitos busca el octavo grande a sus 23 años. Nadie en la historia ganó el Abierto sin haber jugado antes los TMS de Canadá o Cincinnati desde la creación de los torneos Masters 1000 en 1990. Y sólo Federer defendió la corona de Nueva York en este siglo al imponerse en cinco ocasiones seguidas, entre 2004 y 2008. Si alguien es capaz de romper esas estadísticas es el fenómeno de El Palmar.

articles.body: En mitad de la Arthur Ashe de Nueva York, a pregunta de Mary Joe Fernández, extenista y la mujer de Tony Godsick, uno de los hombres más influyentes del tenis como representante de Roger Federer y propietario de la Laver Cup y de la empresa Team8, Carlos Alcaraz confesó que espera poder jugar pronto un dobles con su hermano Jaime. Este es el pequeño de la familia Alcaraz Garfia. A sus 15 años hace tiempo que está demostrando maneras con la raqueta. "Le estoy esperando", dijo el campeón de siete grandes. El día que se produzca esa instantánea para la historia no será la primera con los dos juntos en un mismo lado de la pista. En abril de 2022, con Alcaraz recién coronado como campeón del Godó, tomó un avión destino Atenas para participar en la exhibición Invitacional IMG Future Stars, en el club de tenis TATOÏ. Allí formó pareja con Jaime, que sólo tenía 10 años. Jaime progresa adecuadamente y a finales del pasado mes de marzo se adjudicó el sub'15 de Murcia. La pasada temporada, el campeón de siete grandes coincidió con su hermano pequeño durante la disputa del Godó entre profesionales y sub'14. Y no dudó en grabar con el móvil las evoluciones de Jaime, que cada día va a más. articles.title: ‘Not at Wimbledon’: US Open influencer chaos prompts Grand Slam to rethink creator access
articles.summary: Tennis News: Wimbledon appears to be taking note of the controversy surrounding influencers and content creators at the US Open, with the All England Club planning.
articles.body: Wimbledon appears to be taking note of the controversy surrounding influencers and content creators at the US Open, with the All England Club planning a far more restrictive approach when the Grand Slam returns next summer.According to the Press Association, Wimbledon does not plan to introduce a dedicated accreditation category for influencers or content creators for the 2027 tournament. Security is also expected to confiscate equipment such as ring lights if it is deemed capable of disrupting matches.The move comes as the US Open has grappled with a growing debate over the balance between expanding tennis's audience and protecting the etiquette and atmosphere around matches.The contrast between the two Grand Slams is striking. While the US Open has embraced creators as part of its strategy to reach new audiences, Wimbledon appears ready to draw a much firmer line.US Open's influencer experiment sparks backlashThe US Open credentialed around 100 influencers and content creators this year, almost double the 54 who received credentials in 2025. The initiative was designed to bring the tournament to audiences beyond traditional sports media and strengthen its presence across social platforms.But the increased presence has coincided with several incidents that have put tennis etiquette under the spotlight.Naomi Osaka's first-round match became one of the most prominent examples. A group of spectators in a suite was filming and taking photographs during play, with a bright ring light also involved. Chair umpire Kader Nouni intervened and briefly stopped the match to address the disruption.Osaka subsequently acknowledged the potential benefits of creators while making it clear that there needed to be boundaries."I feel like it's common courtesy to read up on the sport, especially the etiquette. I feel like it could be a good thing for people to make the sport of tennis popular to their specific audience, but I think it has to be managed a lot better, especially in the situation like in my first-round match," Osaka said."Overall, I think there's huge positives. … You want people to continue to grow the sport. I just think it has to be in a way that everyone knows the rules and the etiquette."The controversy has not been limited to influencers. Players have also complained about movement in the stands, noise and other distractions during matches.French veteran Adrian Mannarino was particularly blunt about the atmosphere."People are allowed to move around in the crowd during points," Mannarino said, according to the Press Association. "The tournament puts up with it, and I don't know if it's the best thing for tennis in general."There's a smell of marijuana on the court, noise everywhere. The truth is, it's turning into a bit of a zoo."Wimbledon chooses a different pathThe US Open's experience appears to have offered Wimbledon a warning about how quickly efforts to make a Grand Slam more accessible and social-media friendly can collide with the traditional demands of tennis.The All England Club's decision not to create a specific influencer accreditation category represents a clear departure from the US Open's approach. It is also expected to take a strict stance on equipment such as ring lights and other items that could interfere with play.That does not necessarily mean Wimbledon is turning its back on digital creators. Rather, the approach suggests that the tournament intends to keep content creation within existing expectations around spectator behaviour and match etiquette.Players at the US Open have themselves acknowledged that influencers can help bring new audiences to tennis.Coco Gauff, the 2023 US Open champion, suggested that brands bringing influencers to matches should ensure they understand the basic rules of the sport."Sometimes it's their first tennis match; they don't know. They have probably been to basketball games before," Gauff said."With anything, any venue you go to, if you're being invited to a red carpet, you wouldn't show up in jeans. I think it's just follow the etiquette of the sport."Jessica Pegula also saw the upside of creators showcasing the US Open experience but warned against crossing the line."It's tough when you see videos like that when they're taking pictures and using the selfie lights," Pegula said. "People are down there trying to perform, and it's their career and their job. It seems like a bit disrespectful.""I think it's gotten a little maybe too much, it feels like, this year. I don't know. I think I can appreciate one side of it, but I think when you have the other side literally interrupting matches, it gets a little tough."For Wimbledon, the message from New York appears to be clear: attracting a new generation of fans may be important, but not at the expense of the players' ability to compete without distraction.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: US Open 2026: Why several leading men's contenders have tumbled in New York - and why the women's draw is more stable
articles.summary: The chaotic nature of the men's draw has been a sharp contrast to the relative calm of the women's - but anyone can still win the US Open titles.
articles.body:
Talent, athleticism and commitment are not nearly enough to become a Grand Slam singles champion.

Possessing the confidence that you can beat anyone on the biggest stage - where the eyes of the world are fixed on you and there is no place to hide - is arguably the most important characteristic a player can have.

Unwavering belief. Or, as former US Open runner-up Taylor Fritz describes it, delusion.

Fritz is one of the current crop of leading men yet to get his hands on one of the sport's major prizes. The world number 10 is also one of the guys who has blown what looked like a golden opportunity to win this year's US Open.

With Jannik Sinner missing through injury, and Carlos Alcaraz making his comeback from his long lay-off, it felt like a tournament where the leading seeds could capitalise.

Instead, six of the top 10 perished by the fourth round at Flushing Meadows - including Fritz, who squandered a two-set lead against Argentina's Francisco Cerundolo in round three.

Former champion Daniil Medvedev's fourth-round exit on Sunday means the only top-10 players remaining are top seed Alexander Zverev, defending champion Alcaraz and eighth seed Ben Shelton.

"It shows you how even the circuit is, how tight every match is, how difficult it is to win matches," said 24th seed Cerundolo.

The dominance of Sinner and Alcaraz - who have won 10 of the past 11 Grand Slam men's singles titles between them - adds to the pressure.

Speaking to the Guardian , external earlier this year, 28-year-old Fritz said he believes he will feel an "emptiness" at the end of his career if he does not win a Grand Slam title.

World number two Zverev finally landed his first major at this year's French Open, but revealed afterwards he "could not sleep" and was "not eating" during previous Slam fortnights because of nerves.

Once he released the pressure valve, the 29-year-old German went on to reach the Wimbledon final - where he played freer but still lost to Sinner - and remains in the hunt at the US Open.

Zverev is scrambling through his half of the draw despite being far from his best, but the spectre of Alcaraz - who is getting better with every win - looms large.

"The two-horse race between Sinner and Alcaraz is not healthy for the tour," former Wimbledon champion Pat Cash told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"With every win, Alcaraz is becoming more of a favourite. Four months off, no matches and he could win the US Open."

Are there other reasons behind early exits?

Pressure is not the sole reason for the leading seeds tumbling in New York.

One argument is that the current top 10 - Sinner and Alcaraz aside - is weaker than it has been for a while.

Illness, injuries and fatigue also contributed at the final major of a demanding season.

Fourth seed Novak Djokovic's ageing body let him down in his shock first-round exit, while third seed Felix Auger-Aliassime put his second-round loss down to suffering dizziness.

Fifth seed Flavio Cobolli said he lacked energy in a third-round defeat, which he attributed to his volume of matches and New York's sapping heat.

Cincinnati champion Arthur Fils lost a tough opener against former world number three Stefanos Tsitsipas, while teenager Rafael Jodar - who has played more than 50 matches in his first full season on tour - looked drained during his first-round exit.

"The season is long. I think all the guys who performed well in the preparation tournaments have it more difficult here," said Belgium’s Alexander Blockx, who knocked out French Open finalist Cobolli.

"We're all human. We're not robots. Every week is difficult. Especially at a Grand Slam where it gets even more physical.

"Mentally you have to really stay in it."

The calm amid the chaos - but anyone can also win women's title

The chaotic nature of the men's draw has been a sharp contrast to the calm of the women's.

Eleven of the top 16 seeds reached the fourth round, led by two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka and Australian Open winner Elena Rybakina.

Neither dropped a set on their way to the last 16, while American pair Jessica Pegula and Coco Gauff - seeded third and fourth - progressed without any serious scares.

French Open winner Mirra Andreeva and Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova ensured the top six seeds remained unscathed.

Two-time major finalist Karolina Muchova, Ukraine's Elina Svitolina and 2025 US Open runner-up Amanda Anisimova were the first top-10 seeds to be eliminated when they lost in the third round.

"It is great for the women's tour to have so many people who could possibly win," added Cash.

"Anyone can win at any time - doesn't that make it exciting?"

The past seven Grand Slams have produced seven different winners - a stark contrast to Sinner and Alcaraz's dominance - and leads to a school of thought that the current crop of top stars feel less burden than the men.

Everyone in the top 10 is a reigning Slam or WTA 1,000 champion, underlining their ability to triumph on the biggest stages.

The four leading players locked in a battle at Flushing Meadows for the top ranking adds another element to the dynamic.

Sabalenka has been the world number one for the past two years, but has recently suffered a dip of form which leaves her position under severe threat.

Rybakina is guaranteed to overtake Sabalenka if she reaches the semi-finals, while Pegula and Gauff could pounce if they win the title.

"Looking at the difference between the points in the top 10 compared to the men, you can see how the depth is pretty crazy," said Pegula.

"Everyone has been very consistent and makes it hard to a certain extent [to win a Slam].

"But then you know there's not one or two super dominant players where you feel like they have to lose in order for you to have a chance."

articles.title: Roger Federer’s simple career mantra stunned Golden State Warriors — Steve Kerr saw the same secret in Steph Curry’s pursuit of greatness
articles.summary: Tennis News: Roger Federer’s career was built on numbers that seem almost impossible to comprehend.Twenty Grand Slam titles. One hundred and three tour-level troph.
articles.body: Roger Federer’s career was built on numbers that seem almost impossible to comprehend.Twenty Grand Slam titles. One hundred and three tour-level trophies. Three hundred and ten weeks as the world No. 1, including 237 consecutive weeks at the top. Five successive US Open titles between 2004 and 2008, a record that remains untouched in the Open Era.But years ago, when the Swiss great was asked by a group of Golden State Warriors players how he had managed to sustain that extraordinary level for so long, his answer had remarkably little to do with the usual language of sporting greatness.No talk of outworking everyone. No grand speech about sacrifice. No obsession with being better than the next player. Instead, Federer spoke about something far more ordinary: his daily routine and the joy he found in it.The anecdote has stayed with Warriors coach Steve Kerr ever since.Federer’s remarkable career, in perspectiveFederer, 45, was officially inducted into the International Tennis Hall of Fame on August 29 in Newport, Rhode Island. A few days later, he returned to New York to receive his Hall of Fame ring inside Arthur Ashe Stadium and spent time around the US Open — the tournament where he produced one of the toughest records in modern tennis.Federer won five consecutive US Open titles from 2004 to 2008. He remains the only player, man or woman, to win five straight titles in New York during the Open Era.Yet one of the most revealing stories about his approach to longevity came not from a Grand Slam final or a record-breaking season, but from a conversation with the Warriors during their 2017 trip to China.A question from Draymond GreenFederer was in Shanghai for the Masters tournament when the Warriors invited him to speak to the team.Kerr later recalled how Draymond Green asked the 20-time Grand Slam champion a question that seemed to invite the standard answer about relentless work and sacrifice.“I’ll tell you a great story about Roger Federer. We were playing in China with the Warriors in 2017. Roger was in Shanghai for the Masters tournament, so we invited him to come speak to the team.”“Draymond Green asked him, ‘How do you sustain success? How have you managed to win majors 20 years after you first won one?’ Everyone was expecting him to say, ‘I work harder than everybody,’ the will, all the clichés.”Instead, Federer talked about getting up in the morning, making breakfast for his children, taking them to school and then going to train.Federer’s answer was surprisingly simple“Roger Federer says, ‘I get up every morning and I make breakfast for my kids. Then I take them to school and drop them off. Then I go practice tennis for about two hours, and I’ve figured out a really good routine where I don’t destroy my body, but I can get all the work in I need.’”And then came the line that Kerr remembered most.“‘Then I go have lunch with my wife. In the evening, we cook dinner together. The kids are all home from school. We ask them about school. There’s so much joy in the house. We put them to bed, and then I put my head on the pillow and go, “Man, that was just a great day.” And I’ve been doing that for 20 years.’”For Kerr, the message was striking because Federer had reduced the mystery of sustained excellence to something that sounded almost deceptively simple.“And it was like, yes. That’s it. That’s the formula. That’s what leads to sustained success.”Not just about working harderThe important part was not simply how much Federer trained. It was that he had built a life in which training, competing and everything around it remained something he genuinely enjoyed.“He loves tennis. He loves his family. He loves life.”That was a very different answer from the one the Warriors expected to hear.Instead of presenting longevity as a battle against exhaustion, Federer described a routine that allowed him to keep returning to his craft without losing his enthusiasm for it.Why Federer made Kerr think of CurryYears later, Kerr would draw a parallel between Federer and Stephen Curry — two superstars from entirely different sports who have nevertheless made extraordinary athletic excellence look almost effortless.Federer’s movement around a tennis court and Curry’s movement on a basketball court have a similar visual quality: precision, balance and timing wrapped in an apparent ease that can obscure the work underneath.Kerr sees something deeper connecting them.When asked about Curry’s day-to-day conditioning and what stood out about the way the Warriors star maintained himself, Kerr immediately went back to the idea of routine.Curry’s routine is “like a metronome”“Just the consistency of his routine – it’s like a metronome every day. It’s exactly the same. He is in the training room, he is in the weight room, he’s on the court. It’s clockwork, but there’s also a sense of joy and energy within that work. He enjoys it so much, he loves the process.”For Kerr, that combination of discipline and enjoyment is what separates longevity from simply surviving a long career.“I think that’s one of the things that ties all great athletes together. I’m talking about the superstar athletes, the Roger Federers of the world, the Steph Currys of the world. There’s a routine that is not only super disciplined and is really enjoyed each day.”“There is a passion that comes with it, and that’s what sustains it over time. And when you love something like those guys do, you work at it and you get better and you just keep going…”Curry’s love for the workCurry, when asked about Kerr’s comparison, responded with a touch of humour.“I’ve got to get a list of all the guys he’s compared me to: [Former Spurs star] Tim Duncan, Roger Federer.”But beneath the joke, Curry’s explanation of his own career sounded remarkably close to the philosophy Kerr had remembered from Federer.“I love to work. You kind of get lost in the sessions you have on the court in practice…in the weight room, wherever it is, because you know it’s going to lead to you being as prepared as possible for those games. [I] try to have as much fun as possible…”There are difficult days, Curry acknowledged, but the underlying approach remains the same.“[There are] days you are tired…but it’s all built on my approach from the time I started, and just trying to carry that every year for as long as I can…win, lose, whatever it is, no matter how you play, you have to keep coming back to the well to keep sharpening the toolkit and finding ways to evolve your game.”That philosophy has allowed Curry to keep reinventing himself as his career has progressed.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.summary: El español, que este martes jugará contra Shelton en los cuartos de final del torneo, optó por no ejercitarse y desconectar por las calles de la Gran Manzana
articles.body: Carlos Alcaraz, que tras 139 días sin jugar está protagonizando en el US Open el mejor regreso desde el que firmó Rafa Nadal en 2022, ha optado por no entrenarse en la jornada de este lunes, horas después de su gran victoria de octavos ante Tommy Paul, por 6-4, 6-3 y 6-4. Carlitos prioriza el descanso por segunda vez desde que empezó el torneo. La otra fue el jueves tras el partido de segunda ronda con Jaime Faria y que terminó en la noche neoyorquina. El español, número 3 mundial, ha preferido descansar del tenis, dado que suma ya suficiente rodaje después de más de cuatro meses de inactividad, y ha elegido, según ha podido saber MARCA, dar un paseo por antes de su nuevo compromiso en el último Grand Slam del año. Será, por un día, un turista más en la ciudad de los rascacielos. Por primera vez en mucho tiempo, el campeón de siete grandes ha podido reunir a toda su familia en un mismo evento. Sus padres, Carlos y Virginia, y sus tres hermanos, Álvaro, Sergio y Jaime, le acompañan estos días en su aventura americana. Juanjo Moreno, fisioterapeuta del tenista, siempre destaca la Vitamina N de la naturaleza a la hora de afrontar compromisos importantes como el de este martes en la antepenúltima ronda del Abierto estadounidense. A Caritos le encanta pasear como uno más por Central Park e inmortalizarse con el fondo de los rascacielos junto a los miembros de su equipo. Ayuda que su residencia neoyorquina esté a escasos metros del famoso parque. Con o sin gorra, su rostro es el más conocido de Manhattan. Los 'highlights' de sus puntos se repiten una y otra vez en las pantallas gigantes de Times Square. Fue precisamente Times Square su primera parada en Nueva York, en su debut en el cuarto 'major' del calendario. Posteriormente, visitó el Rockefeller Center, lugar donde la semana pasada estuvieron sus padres y hermanos. También fue en Times Square donde se sacó la foto con el trofeo como campeón de la edición de 2022. Alcaraz, que se enteró a última hora de la noche del domingo que su rival en los cuartos será el local Ben Shelton, volverá a jugar este martes en la central Arthur Ashe en un horario aún por determinar. Shelton ha cedido los tres precedentes con el murciano, el último de ellos en los octavos de Roland Garros 2025. El estadounidense viene en forma, ya que acaba de sumar el título en el Masters 1000 de Montreal en el inicio de la gira americana de pista dura. Carlitos busca en Nueva York el octavo grande a sus 23 años. Nadie en la historia ganó el Abierto sin haber jugado antes los TMS de Canadá o Cincinnati desde la creación de los torneos Masters 1000 en 1990.

articles.title: Lights, camera, action: Irksome influencers at the US Open are here to stay
articles.summary: Experts say influencers likely to remain a feature of major sports events, despite the anger and irritation they cause.
articles.body:
Influencers at this year’s US Open have stolen the spotlight for disrupting play and acting in a way that is antithetical to traditional tennis etiquette, drawing the ire of players and spectators alike.

But despite the pushback and complaints, it looks like they’re here to stay.

Tennis’s biggest stars weren’t battling weather extremes and challenging court surfaces last week when the year’s fourth and final Grand Slam got under way at Flushing Meadows in New York. The disruption, rather, came from flashy ring lights, untimely selfies and raucous behaviour from influencers in the spectator stands.

The use of influencers – social media personalities who create content for followers online – is a relatively new trend in sports marketing across major sporting tournaments like tennis’s US Open and football’s FIFA World Cup.

According to sports media experts, they’re only going to become mainstream and more relevant.

What was the influencer row at the US Open about?

Players aren’t pushing back against influencers, one hundred of whom the US Open has formally accredited this year, so much as they’re calling for respect for the players and the game.

A chair umpire was forced to reprimand influencers for staging a disruptive photo shoot while two-time US Open champion Naomi Osaka was serving during her first-round win against Anastasia Zakharova last Monday.

Another social media user attracted attention for all the wrong reasons when she posted a series of photos posing inside the Arthur Ashe Stadium while Madison Keys was in the middle of playing a point against Alina Korneeva, which breached basic tennis etiquette.

Videos on social media showed people moving about the stands during play or taking group photographs, often without consideration for fans around them trying to enjoy the match.

Why are influencers at the US Open anyway?

Influencers are the latest, and a significantly cost-effective, marketing trend in the sports industry, Leslie Koroma, CEO of Africa Sports Ventures Group, told Al Jazeera.

The sports media expert agreed with the pushback from tennis fans used to the traditional model of informed journalists covering the sport compared to influencers with little to no knowledge.

“But this isn’t going away any time soon; we’re living in a digital, tech age, and this trend will continue,” Koroma said of the influencers, many of whom have millions of followers across TikTok, Instagram, and other social media platforms.

What brands and the US Open itself pay influencers is undisclosed, and it depends on their social media reach and following. It can, however, be safely assumed to be significantly less than the $17m spent on marketing in 2023 and 2024, down from $30m in 2021 and 2022, per the consolidated financial statements of the United States Tennis Association (USTA).

Do influencers add any value to sports tournaments?

Influencers are able to reach audiences that traditional media cannot, according to Nasha Smith, a sports media ethics professor at Arizona State University.

“The biggest thing influencers bring to the table is access to an audience, because tournaments can spend a lot of money trying to reach a particular demographic, while influencers may already have that audience sitting there waiting for their next post, and that can be incredibly valuable from a marketing perspective,” Smith told Al Jazeera.

“And it’s not just about something going viral; influencers can make a tournament feel more accessible or relevant to people who aren’t traditionally sports fans,” she added.

Of the 100 influencers accredited by the US Open, 20 are dedicated to providing coverage of the food and beverage scene alone. Others show what fans are consuming (such as Honey Deuce cocktails and overpriced chicken nuggets topped with caviar), what they’re wearing, and what the overall atmosphere is like.

Is influencer-led marketing just a numbers game?

Smith cautioned against organisers solely using online views and engagement as a rubric for success.

“If the content doesn’t translate into people becoming interested in the sport, attending the events, watching matches or following players, then you definitely have to question what you gained from this collaboration [with influencers],” she said.

Koroma knows that once the dust on this trend settles, marketing experts will evaluate how best to bring influencers into the fold of traditional marketing, although he did caution tournament organisers to think about the eventual outcome of using influencers as a medium to reach fans and the general public at large.

Will we keep seeing influencers at major sports tournaments?

What might seem like an affront to the sanctity of sports will become the new normal, according to experts.

“Sports, like everything else, has always evolved; tournaments have always evolved with their audiences in terms of changing the rules to speed up play or make play more palatable to an audience,” Smith said.

“But there’s a point where creating content starts interfering with the actual event, and I don’t think competition should be sacrificed for engagement,” she added.

“The goal should be to find a way to bring influencers and creators to that environment without making the athletes or other spectators pay the price for it.”

What have players said about the disruption?

“Obviously if you come to a sporting event, you have to respect the sport,” Osaka told reporters after her second-round win over Katerina Siniakova.

The former world number one, along with 2024 runner-up Jessica Pegula, said they were not opposed to influencers making tennis popular to their specific audience, but emphasised the need for decorum at the tournament.

“People are down there trying to perform, and it’s their career and their job. It seems a bit disrespectful,” Pegula said.

Daniil Medvedev, the 2021 champion, said he was all for popularising tennis, but acknowledged that distractions made it “challenging” for athletes to focus on their game.

How has the US Open responded to the incidents?

The disruptions prompted organisers to respond with messages being displayed on court screens that read: “Please refrain from the use of flash photography or other lighting during match play.”

US Open head Brendan McIntyre also clarified that two influencers were incorrectly credentialed and therefore had their access revoked.
