articles.summary: Zheng Qinwen wins a set from 5-0 down for the second successive match as she shocks Iga Swiatek to reach the US Open quarter-finals.
articles.body:
Zheng Qinwen won a set from 5-0 down for the second match in succession as she extended her fantastic US Open run by beating former champion Iga Swiatek to reach the quarter-finals.

Zheng, the reigning Olympic champion and former world number four, dropped outside the world's top 100 earlier this year while struggling to regain her best form following elbow surgery in July 2025.

The 23-year-old from China had trailed Madison Keys 5-0 in the deciding set of their third-round match on Saturday before winning seven successive games to secure her spot in round four.

And Zheng was 5-0 down in the opening set against Poland's eighth seed Swiatek, but won 13 of the next 16 games on Arthur Ashe Stadium to set up a quarter-final against either Naomi Osaka or Elena Rybakina.

The second set was on serve until the seventh game, when Zheng crushed a powerful backhand return winner to secure a crucial break, and she broke again two games later to complete a 7-5 6-3 victory.

This latest win - her seventh in a row in New York having come through three rounds of qualifying - will put her back to the brink of the top 50.

"The more matches I play, the more rhythm I have on court," said Zheng.

"People have asked me if I'm tired and when I arrived I was not tired at all. I felt really pumped for my match, trying to reach better levels here and enjoy this fantastic stadium."

Elsewhere, French Open winner Mirra Andreeva recovered from losing the first set to Anastasia Potapova to reach the last eight in New York for the first time in her career.

'Finally luck is on my side' - Zheng comes from match point down to beat Keys

I can't relate to pressure Eala faces - Gauff

Zheng's only win in eight previous meetings against Swiatek was in the semi-finals of the 2024 Olympics on her way to singles gold in Paris.

She will discover her quarter-final opponent later on Monday, when former US Open champion Osaka plays second seed Rybakina.

The most recent qualifier to reach this stage of the women's draw at the US Open was Great Britain's Emma Raducanu, who went on to win the title in 2021.

And Zheng is not the first female qualifier to perform well at a Grand Slam in 2026 - Poland's Maja Chwalinska, who began the French Open at 114th in the world, lost to Russian teenager Andreeva in the final at Roland Garros.

For Swiatek, 25, a fourth-round exit is a disappointing end to her Grand Slam season, with a quarter-final appearance at the Australian Open her best result.

She was beaten in round four of the French Open, while the defence of her Wimbledon title ended in the third round.

It means that, for the first time since 2021, Swiatek will end a year without winning one of the sport's four majors.

Swiatek, who received treatment to her left thigh when leading 2-1 in the second set, had entered the US Open in excellent form by winning the WTA 1000 event in Toronto and getting to the semi-finals in Cincinnati, while she had progressed through to round four without dropping a set.

Andreeva through against 'warrior' Potapova

Andreeva, 19, was severely tested by Potapova until the 24th seed injured her knee in what proved to be the final game of their match on Louis Armstrong Stadium.

Potapova seemed to twist or hyperextend her knee while attempting to hit a ball on the run from the baseline and Andreeva was across quickly to check on her grounded opponent.

Russia-born Potapova, who represents Austria, returned to the court after receiving treatment but lost the remaining points in her service game, confirming her exit from the tournament.

Fifth seed Andreeva, who won 5-7 6-4 6-3, said: "Anastasia is my good friend and seeing what a battle we had and seeing her fall like that in the last game, it's not easy.

"I told her that she's been playing amazing and having one of her best seasons. I'm sure she'll come back even stronger - she's a warrior and an even better fighter than me."

Andreeva will play either Coco Gauff or Iva Jovic, who play their all-American fourth-round match in Monday's night session, in the quarter-finals.

articles.title: Zheng shocks Swiatek in another incredible US Open comeback
articles.summary: Olympic gold medallist Zheng Qinwen, who had to come through US Open qualifying, stunned six-time Grand Slam champion Iga Swiatek 7-5, 6-3 to reach the quart...
articles.body:
Olympic gold medallist Zheng Qinwen, who had to come through US Open qualifying, stunned six-time Grand Slam champion Iga Swiatek 7-5, 6-3 to reach the quarter-finals on Monday.

It was another gritty win for the Chinese star, a former world number four now ranked 121st in the wake of elbow surgery last year.

Zheng won the last seven games to stun Madison Keys in her previous match.

After falling behind 5-0 in the first set against Swiatek she again reeled off seven straight.

She broke the Polish star twice in the second set to clinch the win over the player she beat in the gold medal match in Paris two years ago.

"I guess to come back from 0-5 yesterday is not lucky, that's all I can say," Zheng said.

"I just focus on point by point," added Zheng, who saved three set points in the opening set.

Zheng, who said it took some time to adjust to the cavernous Arthur Ashe Stadium, made a number of sloppy errors as Swiatek raced to a 5-0 lead.

"Honestly, I have to say I started the match not so well," Zheng said. "Little by little I found my rhythm on the center court because it's been a long, long time. I just really appreciate it to be here in the Ashe Stadium.

"I'm just really happy to win this match because it's not easy, and it's been a while really I didn't beat any top 10 player."

Zheng was already the first qualifier to reach the US Open women's fourth round since Emma Raducanu -- who went on to win the title in 2021.

Next she'll face either world number two Elena Rybakina or two-time US Open winner Naomi Osaka for a place in the semi-finals.

Swiatek left the court in tears after another bitter Grand Slam disappointment.

She won her most recent major at Wimbledon last year but fell in the quarter-finals at the Australian Open in January before a fourth-round exit at Roland Garros and a third-round defeat in her Wimbledon title defense.

articles.title: US Open 2026: Qinwen Zheng makes incredible comeback, upsets Iga Świątek in straight sets
articles.summary: Qinwen Zheng once again rallied with her back against the wall.
articles.body:
Qinwen Zheng needed to dig deep Monday. After trailing 0-5 in the first set to Iga Świątek, Zheng found the strength — again — to rally all the way back and pick up a massive, upset win over the No. 8-ranked player.

Zheng used that momentum to knock off Świątek in straight sets (7-5, 6-3) to advance to the quarterfinals at the US Open.

Things looked extremely promising from Świątek early. After five games, she led 5-0 and looked poised to make quick work of the much, much lower-ranked Zheng. But being down 5-0 in a set is apparently when Zheng plays her best tennis.

For the second-straight match — and in her second-straight set — Zheng somehow rallied from 5-0 to win the next seven games and actually steal the win from Świątek in the first set.

Zheng pulled off the exact same comeback in her third set vs. Madison Keys on Saturday, rallying from down 0-5 to come back and win that set — and match — 7-5.

Zheng played sloppy tennis early, making a number of unforced errors in the first five games against Świątek. In the fifth game, Zheng lost thanks to a double fault and two unforced errors.

From there, she started rolling. Zheng was credited with just two unforced errors over the next seven games. Instead, it was Świątek who suddenly couldn't land her shots.

That set up a potential match-winning opportunity to Zheng in the second set. Despite having all the momentum on her side, Zheng dropped the first game of the second set to Świątek, a sign the No. 8-ranked player wasn't going down that easily. Zheng, however, quickly evened up the set at 1-1 in the next game.

Świątek appeared to be mounting a comeback, taking the third game. But before the fourth game of the second set began, a trainer came out to take a look at Świątek. It was initially unclear what was ailing her.

Świątek continued with the match, but quickly lost the next game, increasing concern about a possible injury. But Świątek took the next game, again evening the set.

From that point, however, Zheng again found her stride, winning the next four games to win the second set. She nearly kept Świątek off the board entirely in the final game, but Świątek had one more late rally in her before eventually falling 6-3 in the set.

Coming into the match, Świątek held a significant advantage. She held a 7-1 record vs. Zheng in their head-to-head matchups. Zheng's only victory in those eight matches came at the Paris Olympics in 2024, when Zheng toppled Świątek in straight sets. Zheng rode that victory all the way to a gold medal at the event.

Despite that win, Zheng entered Monday's match ranked 121st by the WTA. Świątek came into the contest as the WTA's No. 8.

With the win, Zheng will advance to the quarterfinals at the US Open for the third time in her career. She's never advanced past that stage of the tournament, however.

If Zheng is going to continue her miracle run, she'll need to topple yet another strong opponent in the quarterfinals. Zheng will take on the winner of Naomi Osaka and Elena Rybakina, who are set to square off Monday afternoon.

articles.title: US Open 2026: Qinwen Zheng stages epic comeback to stun Iga Swiatek and reach quarter-finals
articles.summary: Qinwen Zheng produces another stunning fightback to knock out former champion Iga Swiatek and reach the US Open quarter-finals; Mirra Andreeva also through to last eight with comeback win over Anastasia Potapova; watch the US Open live on Sky Sports Tennis
articles.body:
Two days on from saving match point while trailing 5-0 in the third set to Madison Keys, Zheng mounted another remarkable fightback on Arthur Ashe.

Swiatek won the first five games but Zheng simply refused to roll over, winning the next seven games to clinch the first set before overpowering her shellshocked opponent to complete an astonishing 7-5 6-3 victory.

A stunned Swiatek never recovered, and the 2022 champion succumbed in straight sets, 7-5 6-3, leaving the court in tears after her campaign unravelled in unthinkable fashion.

The former world No 4 from China, who had come through qualifying after being sidelined by a long-term elbow injury, became the first qualifier to reach the quarter-finals since Emma Raducanu won the tournament in 2021.

Zheng's reward is a last-eight tie against either Naomi Osaka or Elena Rybakina.

"I started the match not so well but I found my rhythm," Zheng said.

"It has been a long, long time since I played on a centre court and I really appreciate being here on Arthur Ashe Stadium.

"I took it point by point and little by little I started to play better and find my game.

"I even forgot the score at 4-5 in the first set, which showed I was focused. To come back from 0-5 is not lucky, that's all I can say."

"It's a straight-set win but it's one of the great comebacks. Go figure. How's that possible? Zheng made it happen.

"Two games in a row, 5-0 down in sets. She got the win against Madison Keys to get the first set today, before completing victory against Swiatek for only the second time in her career."

"The Chinese dream lives on as the qualifier makes it into the final eight."

Potapova in tears after late injury in Andreeva defeat

Anastasia Potapova was in floods of tears as her stay in New York came to an end.

The 25-year-old Austrian won the first set against fifth seed Mirra Andreeva, but, at 5-3 down in the third she badly twisted her knee chasing a forehand down.

Potapova had the knee heavily strapped up and bravely finished the match, but did not win another point as French Open champion Andreeva triumphed 5-7 6-4 6-3.

"Anastasia is a good friend, and seeing what a battle we have and then seeing her fall is not easy," said Russian teenager Andreeva.

"It's not the way you want to finish the match. I just told her she is playing amazing and I'm sure she'll come back even stronger, she's a warrior."

Zheng said it took her some time to settle in on the cavernous Ashe Stadium court, noting it's been "a long, long time" since she'd been scheduled on a main show court.

"I just focus on point by point," Zheng said, adding that she was so focused on the rallies that she lost track of the score at one point.

Zheng is the first qualifier to reach the US Open women's quarter-finals since Emma Raducanu -- who went on to win the title -- in 2021.

She'll next face world number two Elena Rybakina, the reigning Australian Open champion who cruised past Naomi Osaka 6-1, 6-4 in just 66 minutes.

Rybakina is not only chasing a third Grand Slam title, if she beats Zheng to reach the semi-finals she will seize the number one ranking from Aryna Sabalenka -- even if the Belarusian wins a third straight title.

The 21-year-old Blockx's dream US Open debut continued with a gritty 6-3, 4-6, 7-5, 7-5 victory over Argentina's Francisco Cerundolo.

Blockx, who started the year ranked outside the top 100, had upset fifth-ranked Flavio Cobolli in the third round and now is the first Belgian man to reach the last eight at Flushing Meadows.

Fifth-seeded French Open champion Mirra Andreeva advanced with a 5-7, 6-4, 6-3 victory over Anastasia Potapova in an entertaining match marred by an injury to Potapova in the final game.

Potapova was serving to stay in the match when she lost her footing leaning for a ball and fell to the ground in pain.

Andreeva rushed to help her and after receiving treatment on her knee Potapova limped to the finish line.

"Seeing what a battle we had and seeing in the last game her fall like this, it's not easy," Andreeva said. "I can imagine what she's going through and I have goosebumps on my body."

Men's top seed Alexander Zverev was once again slated to close the action on Ashe, taking on 21st-seeded Italian Luciano Darderi.

The French Open champion has become a late-night fixture, playing into the small hours not only in two five-set marathons but also in his three-set third round win over Alejandro Tabilo.

The German is vying to make the US Open quarter-finals for a fifth time while Darderi will make the last eight of a Grand Slam for the first time if he can pull off the biggest win of his career.

Up first under the lights, fourth-seeded former champion Coco Gauff took on 18-year-old fellow American Iva Jovic.

France's Arthur Gea was vying for a slice of Grand Slam history against Botic van de Zandschulp. He could become the first men's lucky loser ever to reach the quarter-finals at a Grand Slam.

articles.title: Rybakina overpowers Osaka to reach U.S. Open quarterfinals
articles.summary: Elena Rybakina outclassed former U.S. Open champion Naomi Osaka on Monday to reach the quarter-finals.
articles.body: Elena Rybakina outclassed former U.S. Open champion Naomi Osaka 6-1 6-4 on Monday to reach the quarterfinals, while China’s Zheng Qinwen ​mounted another extraordinary fightback to upset six-time major winner Iga Swiatek. Two-time major winner ‌Rybakina will face Olympic champion Zheng in the quarterfinals and is now one win away from becoming world No. 1 for the first time. The Japanese 13th-seed Osaka struggled to cope with the Kazakh’s power, hampered ​by an Achilles tendon injury that had flared up in the previous round. Zheng has ​become Flushing Meadows’ most entertaining escape artist this year, coming back from ⁠a 0-5 deficit in the deciding set against third-round foe Madison Keys. She let the first five ​games slip through her fingers in 20 minutes against the 2022 champion Swiatek before digging in, ​and she collapsed to the court with her face in her hands after sealing the win on the fourth match point. Zheng is the first qualifier since Emma Raducanu in 2021 to reach the quarterfinals of the ​women’s draw, as she battles back from a chronic elbow injury that had stunted her ​career. Mirra Andreeva’s entertaining match against Anastasia Potapova ended on a sour note as the Austrian went down injured ‌in ⁠the final game. Potapova valiantly retook the court but could not hold off the inevitable as Andreeva sealed the 5-7, 6-4, 6-3 win with a backhand strike before going across the net to hug her opponent. In the men’s draw, Belgium’s Alexander Blockx continued his breakout run, dispatching Argentine ​24th seed Francisco Cerundolo ​6-3, 4-6, 7-5, 7-5 ⁠to reach his first Grand Slam quarterfinal. Gauff, Zverev highlight evening program The evening action in New York features 2023 champion Coco Gauff in an all-American ​clash against teenage sensation Iva Jovic, before French Open champion Alexander ​Zverev takes ⁠on Luciano Darderi. Italian Darderi beat Zverev at the Rome Masters earlier this year, and he’ll be aiming to repeat that upset when he faces the top men’s seed in the night’s opening match ⁠on Arthur ​Ashe Stadium. Closing out the evening at Louis Armstrong Stadium, ​American Learner Tien takes on Russian Karen Khachanov, hoping to join compatriots Ben Shelton, Frances Tiafoe and Alex Michelsen in ​the last eight.

articles.title: US Open: Coco Gauff bests Iva Jovic in straight sets to return to quarterfinals
articles.summary: Gauff held off the surging American teenager to make her first appearance in the US Open quarterfinal since she won the tournament in 2023.
articles.body:
Three years after winning the US Open, Coco Gauff is making another run. The No. 4 seed defeated 18-year-old Iva Jovic, 6-1, 6-4, in a high-profile battle of young American vs. young American.

Jovic, coming off a huge win over Alex Eala , appeared to be a big challenge for Gauff early on: The 18-year-old picked up a break to open the game, thanks to a handful of unforced errors from Gauff.

But Gauff broke her right back in the next game, after Jovic hit the ball into the net two points in a row. Gauff then went on to win the next five games straight to take the first set 6-1, without much fight from the teenage American.

In the second set, Jovic looked more comfortable, even as Gauff repeatedly threatened to get a break. Gauff finally got the break in the fifth game, pulling Jovic all over the court and giving herself a slight edge. However, Jovic got the break in the next game to even things back up.

Gauff didn't back down, though, breaking Jovic one more time to hang on for a win. This will be the first time that Gauff has appeared in the US Open's quarterfinal since winning the championship in 2023.

Though Jovic showed some fire, the match was essentially Gauff's to lose: The No. 4 seed outplayed Jovic in most stats, and continued her streak of straight-set victories so far in this tournament. Jovic, meanwhile, had 12 unforced errors in the first set alone, ending with 30 unforced errors in total; Gauff also outscored the teenager with 18 winners to Jovic's nine, and 33 (of 59) receiving points, compared to 18 of 50 for Jovic.

The match was billed as a young superstar taking on a potential future superstar, with Jovic impressing in just her third year on the Grand Slam circuit. Gauff, though only 22, had a similar start, but has since gone on to win two Grand Slams and international stardom; some expect Jovic to do the same.

In her postmatch interview, Gauff made a point of shouting out Jovic for her performance, calling her a player who "plays beyond her years."

"I'm sure we'll be playing a lot more matches in the future," Gauff said.

Gauff, though, is the one moving on this time. She will play 19-year-old Russian Mirra Andreeva in the quarterfinals on Tuesday.

articles.title: Carlos Alcaraz gets into groove, beats local favourite Tommy Paul to reach US Open quarterfinals
articles.summary: Tennis News: NEW YORK CITY: There was a moment early in the US Open fourth-round match when Tommy Paul was pulled wide, he lunged forward and, out of nowhere, slam.
articles.body: NEW YORK CITY: There was a moment early in the US Open fourth-round match when Tommy Paul was pulled wide, he lunged forward and, out of nowhere, slammed a forehand winner around the post, landing it behind a stunned Carlos Alcaraz. The crowd gasped, and a flicker of a smile crossed Paul's face. That was the kind of tennis the 29-year-old needed to produce just to make the match competitive against the defending champion.Instead, it was Alcaraz's forehand that lit up Arthur Ashe. The Spaniard ripped it from just about anywhere on the court, threading the needle and neutralising the American's serve as much through positioning as timing. The second seed finished with 33 winners, 17 of them off the forehand side.The world No. 3, returning from a four-month injury-enforced break, advanced to the quarter-finals with a statement 6-4, 6-3, 6-4 win, having dropped just one set across four matches.Sunday was the pair's ninth meeting, with Alcaraz now leading the head-to-head 7-2. Paul, the world No. 21, had won two of their first three meetings back in 2022-23, but on Sunday he admitted he was nowhere near the level required."It sucks! It felt like he's playing at a completely different level than me. It sucks, because you feel like, sh@#t!" Paul said. "But at the same time, you learn a lot every time you play him. Every time I've played him, we've gone to the practice court with new ideas of what he does well and what I can try and put into my game."The practice court had also played a part in Alcaraz's own turnaround in the first week.After his third-round win over China's Yibing Wu, in which he had managed just nine winners off his forehand while making 19 unforced errors on the same side, the Spaniard went back to work."For a tennis player, it's really important how you go to bed in terms of feeling. Especially when you win the match, but you don't feel like you've been hitting the ball well, it is better to go back to the practice court and then just hit for five-ten minutes. Just to hit some balls when you're not nervous or you're not thinking about anything else. Leave the site with a good feeling."Alcaraz left Flushing Meadows feeling a lot better about his forehand on Friday."I think everybody saw the difference in my forehand today," he said.The 23-year-old, who exchanged his espresso-brown gear for a black-and-white look, also noted that his Grand Slam off-days now look very different from previous years.Golf had been his favourite escape when he wanted to get away from the pressure of the tennis court. But after the wrist injury, he cannot risk putting his wrist through the demands of the game. These days, his downtime is about recovery and preparing for the next round.Alcaraz will play the eighth-seeded American Ben Shelton next in the last-eight on Tuesday. The 23-year-old moved past Stefanos Tsitsipas 6-2, 6-3, 6-4 and is into his sixth major quarter-final and his second at Flushing Meadows, where he made the semi-finals in 2023.Meanwhile, Frances Tiafoe shocked 2021 champion Daniil Medvedev 7-6 (1), 6-4, 7-6 (6) to earn one of his biggest wins of the season.The 28-year-old world No. 12, roared on by the home crowd, was pumped up for his clash on Louis Armstrong Stadium as he reached the quarter-finals in New York for the fourth time.The two-time US Open semifinalist had lost six of his previous seven meetings with Medvedev, but was the sharper and more focused of the two through the two-hour, 57-minute contest. Tiafoe will face compatriot Alex Michelsen in the last-eight.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Alex Eala could face heavy WTA punishment after choosing Philippines at Asian Games over China Open
articles.summary: Tennis News: Alex Eala may face significant fines and ranking impacts for choosing to represent the Philippines at the Asian Games instead of playing in the China Open, despite her federation seeking an exemption from the WTA.
articles.body: Alex Eala could face a fine and ranking consequences after choosing to represent the Philippines at the Asian Games instead of competing at the China Open, although her federation has formally asked the WTA to grant her an exemption.The decision comes after Eala's impressive run at the 2026 US Open, where she reached the third round before losing to American teenager Iva Jovic at Arthur Ashe Stadium. She has now confirmed that her next tournament will be the Singapore Tennis Open, before she heads to Japan to represent the Philippines at the Asian Games.Eala explained after her US Open defeat that the opportunity to compete for her country was too important to pass up.Eala chooses Asian Games over China OpenSpeaking to the media after her loss to Jovic, Eala confirmed that she expects to play in Singapore before joining the Philippine team at the Asian Games.“Yes, before (Asian Games) I believe, I will be in Singapore,” Eala said, via Tennis Head.“But yeah, I love playing and competing with the Philippines team and in the SEA, the Asian Games I've also done, I think it's a really fun environment, I love being with the team.”Eala added: “Especially this last SEA Games in December, I had such a great time and I think they're really memories that will stick with me.“You know, the Asian Games happens once every four years and yeah, I just found myself drawn to compete in that over other stuff.”That commitment means Eala will miss the 2026 China Open in Beijing, which is scheduled to take place later this month at around the same time as the Asian Games.According to the Daily Tribune, Eala is one of only two players inside the women's top 20 rankings who will miss the China Open, with world No.15 Victoria Mboko currently sidelined by injury.Eala's decision could therefore leave her facing potential punishment from the WTA.According to Tennis365, the China Open is a WTA 1000 event, making it one of the tournaments regarded as mandatory for players ranked high enough to qualify. The WTA's rules allow players to miss mandatory events in certain circumstances, including injury, other medical issues and personal reasons.Players who miss such an event without an applicable exemption can receive zero ranking points for the tournament. The effect on Eala's ranking, however, would depend partly on how other players perform at the US Open and Singapore Open.She could also face a $10,000 fine, according to the WTA's 2026 rulebook. That is the reported late-withdrawal fine for players ranked between 11th and 25th.Whether the Asian Games will qualify Eala for an exemption remains unclear.PHILTA asks WTA to protect Eala from punishmentThe Philippine Tennis Association (PHILTA) has already formally approached the WTA over the matter, requesting that Eala be exempted from the penalties because she will be representing her country.PHILTA secretary-general John Tiangco, who is also the mayor of Navotas City, confirmed the request to GMA Network.“We have formally informed the WTA that Alex will be representing the Philippines at the Asian Games and have requested an exemption so she will not be penalized for missing a WTA 1000 event,” Tiangco said.“Alex herself has made it clear that representing the Philippines is an honor and that she is choosing to play for the flag,” he added.“We fully support that decision and are doing everything we can to ensure that choosing to represent her country does not come at the expense of her standing on the WTA Tour.”Eala has plenty of experience representing the Philippines on the international stage. She is a two-time Asian Games bronze medallist, having finished third in both the women's singles and mixed doubles, and she won gold in the women's singles at the 2025 Southeast Asian Games in Thailand.Her decision comes during the best period of her professional career so far.Eala won her first WTA singles title in Washington D.C. in August and has climbed to a career-high No.18 in the world rankings. Her run at the US Open was also her best finish at the tournament, with her campaign ending against Jovic in the third round.Her rapid rise has made Eala one of the biggest emerging names in women's tennis, with her US Open appearance even contributing to a significant surge in ticket prices as fans rushed to watch the Filipina compete on one of the sport's biggest stages.The China Open would have offered another major opportunity, with the WTA 1000 event carrying valuable ranking points and bringing together many of the world's leading players.Instead, Eala has chosen the Asian Games.The decision now rests with the WTA, which will determine whether her commitment to representing the Philippines provides sufficient grounds for an exemption from the penalties associated with missing the mandatory Beijing tournament.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.body: NEW YORK: Maaya Rajeswaran Revathi, the 15th seed, made a confident start to her US Open girls' singles campaign, seeing off 15-year-old American Emery Combs in the first round.The 17-year-old Indian got off to a quick start against the world No. 92, racing to a 4-0 lead, but Combs fought back to take the next two games. Maaya then reeled off seven successive games, taking a 5-0 lead in the second set when the American broke while the 15th seed was serving for the match.Maaya closed out 6-2, 6-2 win in 70 minutes."I'm happy to get past the first round, which is always tough," she said. "This is the first time I'm playing her, I didn't know my opponent really well. I was a little nervous when I went in, but I think I'm happy that I got past all that and overall played a good match."Maaya will play qualifier Arina Malygina of Russia in the second round.It was not the best day on the courts for Arnav Paparkar, who went down 4-6, 1-6 to 12th-seeded American Andrew Johnson in the boys' singles first round.Paparkar, ranked No. 18 in the world, struggled with his serve, landing just 52 per cent of his first serves and hitting six double faults. He could convert just three of 10 break-point opportunities in the match, while the American made six of eight."My biggest weapon was not working today, I've been struggling with it the last couple of weeks. I haven't been able to work out what the problem is," Paparkar said. "He has a great backhand, I knew that, so I was attacking his forehand, but without my best shot I couldn't do much damage."In the men's doubles, Sriram Balaji and American Evan King went down fighting to 12th seeds Edouard Roger-Vasselin of France and Hugo Nys of Monaco, losing 4-6, 5-7 in a second-round clash.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Alcaraz desvela su plan para alargar más de una década su carrera: "Necesito cuidar mi salud mental y mi cuerpo"
articles.standfirst: Carlos Alcaraz planea descansos más largos para que su carrera "dure los próximos 10 ó 15 años"
articles.summary: Carlos Alcaraz planea descansos más largos para que su carrera "dure los próximos 10 ó 15 años"
articles.body: Carlos Alcaraz (23 años), que tras superar una larga lesión de muñeca lucha por alcanzar su mejor versión en el US Open, ha reconocido que quiere que su carrera "dure mucho tiempo" y planea tomarse descansos más largos para mantenerse sano física y mentalmente. El tenista murciano explicó ante los medios que gestionaría su calendario con mayor cautela en el futuro y se saltaría algunos torneos. Alcaraz explicó que no está obsesionado con tomarse un descanso en un momento determinado, sino que lo hará siempre que sienta que lo necesite. "No lo sé. Depende. El tenis puede ser muy impredecible porque no sabes cuántos partidos vas a ganar; si los torneos durarán un partido o siete. Nunca se sabe. Dependerá de cómo me sienta física y mentalmente, y de si necesito descansos largos a principios, mediados o finales de año", declaró tras el partido del US Open en el que se impuso a Wu Yibing en tercera ronda. Para asegurarse de estar en condiciones de jugar la próxima década, "quiero jugar los próximos 10 ó 15 años", subrayó que "necesito cuidar mi salud mental y mi cuerpo". "Ya veremos. Porque realmente quiero que mi carrera sea muy larga, que dure los próximos 10 ó 15 años. Simplemente quiero cuidar mi salud mental y mi cuerpo. Ahora mismo... si quiero mantener una carrera tan larga... no lo sé. Dependerá de las circunstancias. De lo que sí estoy seguro es de que me lo tomaré con calma", apuntó el siete veces campeón de un Grand Slam. Alcaraz ya adelantó que "en el futuro voy a tomarme descansos, descansos largos" tras ganar al portugués Jaime Faria por 4-6, 6-0, 6-3 y 6-2 en segunda ronda del US Open. "Quizás no cuatro meses, pero sí uno o dos, saltándose algunos torneos, porque es imposible jugarlos todos", comentó el español. Carlos Alcaraz se mostró cansado tras su victoria ante Tommy Paul en octavos de final del US Open. "Estoy sudando mucho, no he comido nada y me siento un poco mal. Voy a comerme un burrito...", comentó.

articles.title: Coco Gauff dismantles Iva Jovic to reach quarter-finals in confident US Open run
articles.summary: Coco Gauff continued her serene march through the US Open women’s draw with her most complete performance yet on Monday night, seeing off fellow American Iva...
articles.body:
Coco Gauff continued her serene march through the US Open women's draw with her most complete performance yet on Monday night, seeing off fellow American Iva Jovic 6-1, 6-4 to reach the last eight in New York for the first time since winning it all in her grand slam breakthrough three years ago.

The fourth-seeded Gauff overwhelmed Jovic with the depth of her returns and an assured blend of aggression and defense, finishing with twice as many winners (18 to nine) and half as many unforced errors (15 to 30). The 1hr 20min clinic was the latest statement in a late-summer win streak that has transformed her from a player searching for answers this time last year into perhaps the most dangerous woman remaining in the field.

Next comes a delicious quarter-final clash with Mirra Andreeva, the reigning French Open champion and fifth seed, after the 19-year-old Russian came from behind to defeat Anastasia Potapova 5-7, 6-4, 6-3 in Monday's day session.

"The biggest difference in the way I've been playing is just trying to play with no regrets," Gauff said afterwards. "I think I have a lot more fun and success playing like this."

The 22-year-old arrived in New York fresh off her first title of the year in Cincinnati and had yet to drop a set throughout the first week, but Monday's task with barely an empty seat inside Arthur Ashe Stadium represented her stiffest examination yet.

Jovic, the 18-year-old from Los Angeles seeded 14th, has been tabbed as one of the brightest prospects in US tennis since crashing the Australian Open quarter-finals in January ahead of fourth-round runs at both Roland Garros and Wimbledon, which made her the youngest American to reach the second week at three majors in a season since Venus Williams in 1998. She had punched her ticket to the last 16 after a grueling three-hour win over breakout star Alexandra Eala in a Saturday night blockbuster, fighting back from 2-4 down in the deciding set to prevail 7-5, 3-6, 7-5.

Gauff knew first-hand what sort of resistance to expect. Their only previous meeting on tour, at the Rome Open in May, required nearly three hours and a comeback from a set down before Gauff escaped 5-7, 7-5, 6-2 after saving a match point. "I think that experience helped me for today," Gauff said. "I knew to expect that she was going to be at 100 from the first point to the last."

This time there was considerably less drama. After opening with a tense 11-minute exchange of breaks, Gauff never let Jovic get comfortable, taking the ball early off both wings and peeling off six straight games to take the opening set in 33 minutes.

Jovic finally interrupted Gauff's momentum in the middle of the second set, breaking for 3-2, but the fightback proved brief. Gauff broke back immediately and soon after produced her cleanest return game of the night in racing to love-40 before Jovic sent a forehand long for 5-4. Serving for the match, she rattled off four straight points from love-30, sealing the match when Jovic sent a backhand into the net.

"I think I'm doing a good job of when I maybe miss opportunities or lose some games, just keeping it in the past and focusing on the present," said Gauff, who extended streaks of nine straight victories and 20 consecutive sets won. "I don't view it as opportunities lost sometimes. I try to just view it as what to do better and just trusting that I'll be in the same position again."

For Gauff, the self-belief lifting her game is less about any one stroke than the range of solutions at her disposal. "I think that gives me confidence knowing that I have probably, up to this point, like, a plan D," she said. "There's comfortability in having options. If plan A doesn't work, there's B, there's C and there's D."

The contrast with Gauff's position 12 months ago remains night and day. She entered last year's US Open amid an emergency reconstruction of her serve before bowing out quietly against Naomi Osaka in the fourth round. Since then, her work with biomechanics expert Gavin MacMillan has gradually taken hold, including personal-best runs to the semi-finals at Wimbledon and in Canada before her Cincinnati triumph.

The stakes extend beyond a second US Open crown and third major title. Gauff also remains in the hunt to reach the world No 1 ranking for the first time if she wins the tournament and Elena Rybakina, who overpowered Osaka to reach the quarter-finals earlier Monday, fails to win her next match. For now, the immediate order of business is Andreeva and a place in the last four. Gauff has won all five of their previous meetings, though she insisted the head-to-head ledger belies what little separates them on the court.

"Mirra is someone that I always have tough matches with," Gauff said. "They've leaned my way, but I think every match could have almost gone either way. She's obviously in a different mindset now, at the top of the game coming off of a grand slam win. I think it's going to be a really athletic, tough match. Hopefully I can take my opportunities when I get them."
authors: Bryan Armen Graham at Flushing Meadows

articles.title: US Open 2026 results: Lucky loser Arthur Gea is beaten by Botic van de Zandschulp in New York classic
articles.summary: France's Arthur Gea held match point to become the first lucky loser to reach a Grand Slam quarter-final - three hours later he was out of the US Open.
articles.body:
France's Arthur Gea was one point away from being the first lucky loser to reach a Grand Slam quarter-final - but three hours later he was out of the US Open.

Gea, 22, was unable to convert a match point in a third-set tie-break against Dutch opponent Botic van de Zandschulp, then could not serve out victory in the fourth set of a gruelling fourth-round contest.

Van de Zandschulp took full advantage to escape from the jaws of defeat, going on to secure a 3-6 6-7 (0-7) 7-6 (9-7) 7-6 (7-3) 6-4 win after five hours and 13 minutes - the fourth longest match on record at Flushing Meadows.

World number 87 Gea was not ranked high enough for the main draw when the US Open entry list was finalised, meaning he had to go through qualifying instead.

Seeded first, he lost to American Nishesh Basavareddy in the third and final round but earned a reprieve when 2022 finalist Casper Ruud withdrew injured on the eve of the tournament.

Gea took full advantage by beating Argentina's Juan Manuel Cerundolo, Zachary Svajda of the United States and another American Michael Zheng to reach the last 16.

But he could not find a way past 70th-ranked Van de Zandschulp, who said he had "no clue" how he completed a "crazy comeback".

After becoming the 13th lucky loser to be eliminated in the fourth round of a Slam, Gea will receive $480,000 in prize money - a considerable increase on the $66,000 which he thought he was taking home from qualifying.

Gauff's statement win completes stacked US Open line-up

Zverev unsure 'what to do' after finishing before midnight

Van de Zandschulp's reward for reaching the second US Open quarter-final of his career is a meeting with German top seed Alexander Zverev.

Zverev, 29, had a rare finish before midnight in New York when he beat Italian 21st seed Luciano Darderi 6-2 6-2 7-6 (7-3) to reach the last eight.

Zverev's previous three matches finished at 1:55am, 2:15am and 1:09am.

"I don't know what to do with myself because it's before midnight - I might go back to the practice courts or go to a bar," Zverev joked.

On whether he wants to play Van de Zandschulp in Wednesday's night session, the French Open champion added: "I will request the night match for sure.

"I've rented this court out from 11pm until 2am for two weeks so I hope they will continue putting me on at [night] time."

Earlier on Monday, Belgium's Alexander Blockx said he was "really close" to retiring injured against Argentina's Francisco Cerundolo before playing on to reach his first major quarter-final.

Blockx, seeded 28th, fought through rib pain to win 6-3 4-6 7-5 7-5, becoming the first Belgian man to make the last eight in New York.

"It was really tough from the beginning of the match. I was struggling a lot, especially while serving. It kept getting worse throughout the match," said 21-year-old Blockx.

"I was really close to retiring, to be honest. I was just hanging in there, but if I would have lost the third set, I think the chances were really high of me retiring.

Presuming he is fit enough, Blockx will play Russian world number 50 Karen Khachanov in the quarter-finals on Wednesday.

Khachanov, 30, fought back to win 7-5 4-6 6-7 (6-8) 6-1 6-4 against 14th seed Learner Tien, ending the American's attempt to put four home men in the quarter-finals for the first time since 1995.

articles.body: Stefanos Tsitsipas, que con su derrota ante Ben Shelton en cuartos del US Open dejó por primera vez en 150 años unas semifinales del Grand Slam sin un jugador con revés a una mano, compartió una simpática anécdota con un taxista en Nueva York. "Dile a Tsitsipas que deje de ir al baño como si estuviera buscando Narnia", le comentó el taxista al tenista griego, que se hizo pasar por un turista de Oslo amigo de Tsitsipas. "Un conductor de taxi en Nueva York me preguntó si conocía a Stefanos Tsitsipas". "Le dije: 'Somos muy amigos'". "Me respondió: 'Bien. Dile que deje de ir al baño como si estuviera buscando Narnia'". "Me puse la capucha y fingí ser un turista de Oslo". , ningún jugador con revés a una mano alcanzará las semifinales de un Grand Slam.
